title: Annuities, lifecycle cost, equivalent annual cost

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: An option has a lifecycle cost of $1,000k and a life of 20 years, and the rate is 7%. What is its equivalent annual cost?

options.text: $50.0k, the lifecycle cost divided by the twenty years of life
options.says: Dividing by the life ignores the cost of money tied up; the page says the divisor is the annuity factor, not the years.

options.text: $70.0k, the lifecycle cost times the 7% rate for every year
options.says: Cost times rate is the payment of a perpetuity (PV = A/r); over 20 years the payment must also repay the cost.

options.text: $1,000.0k, the lifecycle cost itself, as each year's service costs
options.says: The lifecycle cost is the present value of the whole life, not a yearly cost.

options.text: $94.4k, the level payment over twenty years with the same value
options.says: Right: 1,000 / a(0.07, 20) = 94.39, which the page also gets from npf.pmt.

origin.section: Equivalent Annual Cost Compares Options With Different Lives

questions.stem: Option P has a lifecycle cost of $900k over a 12-year life; option Q has $1,400k over a 30-year life. A colleague picks P because its lifecycle cost is lower. What does the page say about that choice?

options.text: It stands, since a lower lifecycle cost means a lower cost of service
options.says: The page calls this the most common mistake: the two costs buy different numbers of years.

options.text: It is undecided, since the two costs buy different spans of service
options.says: Right: lifecycle costs of options with different lives are not comparable; convert each to EAC.

options.text: It is reversed, since dividing each cost by its life shows Q is cheaper
options.says: Cost divided by life ignores the time value of money; the page rules that shortcut out.

options.text: It stands, since the shorter option can be repeated at no extra cost
options.says: Each repeat costs as much again; the page's four-repair chain costs four lifecycle costs, discounted.

origin.section: Lifecycle Cost Is Every Cost of Owning the Asset, Discounted to One Date

questions.stem: An EAC comparison favours repairing an old breaker (EAC $40k, 5-year life) over replacing it (EAC $46k, 30-year life). Engineering then says the breaker cannot be repaired a second time. What should the analysis do?

options.text: Keep the EAC verdict, since EAC already allows for the shorter life
options.says: EAC allows for the shorter life only by assuming the repair repeats like for like, which engineering just ruled out.

options.text: Keep the EAC verdict, since the lower yearly cost settles the comparison
options.says: The yearly cost is valid only under the like-for-like assumption, which no longer holds.

options.text: Redo it with present values of the actual sequence over one horizon
options.says: Right: when the option cannot repeat, the page says to build the actual sequence over a common horizon and compare present values.

options.text: Redo it with each lifecycle cost divided by its own life in years
options.says: Dividing by the life is the shortcut the page refutes; it ignores the cost of money tied up.

origin.section: Equivalent Annual Cost Assumes the Option Is Repeated Like for Like

concepts: EAC assumes each option is followed by an identical one, and present values over a common horizon replace it when that fails
the yearly figure for a given cost, life and rate
what to do when an option cannot be done again
whether a lower whole-life figure settles a choice between assets lasting different spans
